Environmental Patterns Associated with Coral Bleaching Severity: A Principal Component Analysis¶

Integrated technical report and reproducible study notebook · Study period: 1998 onward

This report connects data description, preparation, PCA, interpretation and validation in one executable sequence. The selected figures and tables are integrated within the relevant report sections. The source data are read-only; derived preparation files are written to processed/ and analytical outputs to outputs/.

Abstract

Coral survey datasets contain correlated environmental measurements that can obscure the patterns associated with bleaching severity. This study asks whether principal component analysis (PCA) can provide an interpretable summary of those patterns. The analysis used 23,069 sampling events from 1998–2019 and 35 environmental inputs. Sampling events were consolidated, remaining input gaps were median-imputed, and selected power transformations and standardisation preceded PCA. Parallel analysis guided component retention; bleaching-group contrasts, source stratification and sensitivity checks supported interpretation. The 7 retained components explained 75.9% of environmental variance. The strongest pooled High-versus-Low score differences were PC4: δ = +0.47; PC3: δ = +0.44. The components summarise environmental variation but do not fully preserve observed bleaching-related separation. Original indicators should therefore be retained alongside PCA summaries, and associations should be validated across independent sources and periods before operational use.

1. Introduction¶

Coral bleaching observations have been assembled across survey programmes, regions and years, with environmental measurements describing thermal conditions, anomalies, accumulated stress and local site characteristics. Differences in measurement schemes and the number of related thermal variables make a direct reading of the pooled dataset difficult (van Woesik & Kratochwill, 2022). A compact description could help identify recurring environmental patterns while making the limitations of a heterogeneous observational database visible.

The primary research question is:

Can principal component analysis reveal major environmental patterns associated with coral bleaching severity?

The objectives are to describe the environmental covariance structure, identify which components and original indicators distinguish bleaching groups, and examine sensitivity to source composition, repeated sites, imputation and time. PCA is appropriate for summarising correlated measurements on continuous scales (Jolliffe & Cadima, 2016). Its components maximise environmental variance; they are not chosen to predict bleaching.

The study uses the requested 1998-onward scope. This is a study-period restriction rather than a rule that earlier observations are invalid. Source documentation notes sparse early coverage; the findings nevertheless apply to the retained labelled cohort, not all reefs or all historical years. Bleaching enters the analysis after PCA as an outcome for interpretation. Associations in these retrospective observations do not establish causal environmental effects or operational warning thresholds.

Execution. Run all cells from the project directory using the environment in requirements.txt, or run python scripts/execute_notebook.py consolidated_report_integrated.ipynb. The latter also refreshes the opening abstract and exports an HTML reading copy. The following settings are the single configuration point for the complete workflow.

2. Dataset and Data Description¶

2.1 Provenance and collection¶

The input is the Version 2 BCO-DMO dataset Bleaching and environmental data for global coral reef sites from 1980–2020 (van Woesik & Burkepile, 2022), associated with the Global Coral-Bleaching Database publication (van Woesik & Kratochwill, 2022). Its archive file is named global_bleaching_environmental.csv; the local copy is named coral.csv. The MD5 check below establishes that the local file is byte-for-byte identical to the archive item whose published MD5 is 42a6f10a6efa9e6b926d04b86b45a19f. A separate SHA-256 fingerprint checks preservation during execution. The dataset is distributed under CC BY 4.0. Table 2 summarises the documented collection schemes and the two small source labels whose protocols remain undocumented.

Table 1 describes the raw export by its actual source labels. Counts of substrate records, sampling events and sites are distinct quantities; they should not be compared as if they shared the same unit of observation. The publication's database-wide record totals use its own presentation and do not replace the dimensions of this particular flattened export.

RAW_HASH = file_sha256(ROOT / "coral.csv")
with (ROOT / "coral.csv").open("rb") as source_stream:
    raw_md5 = hashlib.file_digest(source_stream, "md5").hexdigest()
assert (
    raw_md5 == "42a6f10a6efa9e6b926d04b86b45a19f"
), "Input differs from the cited archive version."
raw = load_raw(ROOT / "coral.csv")
dictionary = load_dictionary(ROOT / "data_dictionary.md")
typed, token_audit = normalise_types(raw)
raw_profile = raw_data_profile(raw, typed, dictionary)
raw_sources = source_collection_summary(typed)
print(
    f"Verified archive copy: {len(raw):,} substrate records, {raw.shape[1]}"
    f" fields, {raw.Sample_ID.nunique():,} sampling-event IDs."
)
source_display = raw_sources.assign(

)

Different observation schemes and severity encodings motivate source-stratified interpretation. Detailed transect lengths or colony rules for AGRRA/FRRP are not inferred beyond the cited compilation description.

Environmental metrics include CoRTAD Version 6 temperature/anomaly products associated with survey locations and times (Saha et al., 2018). The compilation describes MODIS-Aqua Kd490 turbidity at 4-km resolution, summarised within a 100-km buffer using mid-2002–2017 imagery, and IBTrACS cyclone frequency over 1964–2014 (van Woesik & Kratochwill, 2022). These products have different temporal windows; an environmental summary is not necessarily a contemporaneous field measurement.

2.2 Observation structure, variables and study coverage¶

Sample_ID identifies a sampling event and Site_ID identifies a site. Multiple substrate rows can represent the same event, and repeated events can share a site. The raw export contains identifiers, dates, coordinates, source/geographic descriptors, comments, bleaching and cover measurements, and 37 environmental candidate fields. The primary feature set ultimately contains 35 environmental measurements; categories, comments, outcomes and other metadata remain available.

The combined processed table retains 60 source fields plus the bleaching group and missing-depth flag. The two substrate-specific fields are preserved in a separate table linked by Sample_ID. The final cohort contains 23,069 events from 1998–2019, with geographic coverage documented by the coordinates and source summaries. This is not a balanced global monitoring panel.

Some nominally numeric fields arrive as text because nd is embedded among numbers. Source composition and missing-depth percentages in Table 1 already indicate that completeness varies across programmes. Thermal metrics also have blocks of joint missingness. The investigation below documents these patterns before choosing imputation; it does not establish a complete causal missingness mechanism or prove missing-at-random assumptions.

Date precision and units. The source explicitly substitutes day 15 when month and year are known but day is unknown (van Woesik & Kratochwill, 2022); day-level interpretation is therefore avoided. Catalog labels for ClimSST and temperature summaries state °C while their stored values are Kelvin-like. Temperature_Kelvin is explicitly Kelvin. The stored values are preserved, the label discrepancy is disclosed, and no speculative conversion is applied. Windspeed is labelled metres/hour by the source and requires verification before physical interpretation. Standardisation supports covariance analysis but does not resolve uncertain physical labels.

3. Methodology¶

3.1 Study workflow¶

Figure 1 connects the data's substrate grain to the study's event-level environmental PCA. The bleaching outcome is excluded from PCA fitting and introduced later for interpretation. Modules hold the reusable implementations; the calls below execute the complete workflow in this notebook.

figures["study_workflow"] = workflow_figure()
display_figure(
    figures["study_workflow"],
    1,
    "Problem-specific workflow from substrate records to environmental"
    " interpretation",
    "Source categories and comments are retained as metadata. The 1998-onward"
    " and observed-outcome restrictions define the analytical population; PCA"
    " uses 35 environmental inputs.",
)

3.2 Cleaning and cohort selection¶

Known numeric fields are parsed explicitly; unexpected tokens and non-finite values raise errors. Percentages, coordinates and basic measurement ranges are checked. Exact duplicate records, if present, are removed before within-event aggregation. Environmental fields and non-outcome metadata must agree within Sample_ID, including missingness; conflicting fields stop execution. Substrate name and cover are kept in a separate detail table because their multiple event-level values cannot be reduced by an arbitrary first-row choice.

Differing recorded bleaching percentages within an event are averaged, preserving the earlier unweighted aggregation decision. No supplied weights justify a more specific weighting scheme. Distinct event IDs are retained even when other values coincide. Events without observed bleaching are excluded to preserve the labelled study design, and the outcome is never imputed. This is a cohort restriction: PCA itself does not require an observed outcome.

Dates must parse and agree with the recorded year/month/day. Events dated 1997 or earlier are excluded by the inclusive 1998 cutoff. Severity definitions are fixed: Low 0–10%, Moderate >10–50%, High >50–100%, including zeros in Low. Source comments identify mild/moderate/severe code ranges; some percentages are converted codes rather than measurements with equal precision.

Among environmental candidates, SSTA_Mean is constant and TSA_Standard_Deviation has absolute Spearman correlation ≥0.999 with the retained temperature standard deviation. They remain in the combined CSV in original units but are excluded from PCA, as documented in Table 5. Other correlated families are retained. Categories such as Exposure are not assigned artificial numeric scales; the dictionary's “Sometimes” class is not a measured midpoint. Free text, including outcome-derived comments, is retained only as metadata. Events missing more than 50% of the 35 inputs are excluded before fitting medians or transformations. Table 4 distinguishes record consolidation from event exclusion.

measurement_checks = validate_measurements(typed)
events, grain_audit, outcome_conflicts = collapse_samples(typed)
labelled = validate_dates(retain_labelled_samples(events))
period_events, year_exclusions = filter_samples_from_year(
    labelled, SETTINGS["minimum_year"]
)
features, excluded_environmental, correlated_pairs = select_features(
    period_events, SETTINGS["near_duplicate_rho"]
)
roles = column_roles(raw.columns, dictionary, excluded_environmental)
missing_before = missingness_table(period_events, features)
eligible, sparse_exclusions = filter_sparse_samples(
    period_events, features, SETTINGS["max_missing_fraction"]
)
retention = cohort_audit(raw, events, labelled, period_events, eligible)
audit_display = retention.drop(
    columns=["rule", "percent_of_distinct_events"]
).rename(

3.3 Missingness, transformation and validation¶

Figure 2 documents missingness in the period-eligible labelled cohort before sparse-profile exclusion. Source-related depth gaps are investigated using source profiles; retained-event depth-imputation rates accompany the source composition in Table 11. Sparse thermal profiles are excluded because a mostly imputed profile would contain little event-specific information. Remaining input gaps are filled with column medians on the retained cohort; depth imputation is recorded in Depth_m_was_missing, which is not a PCA input. Source relationships and the true missingness mechanism remain limitations.

Inputs with absolute sample skewness >0.75 receive Yeo–Johnson transformation, which permits zeros and negative anomalies (Yeo & Johnson, 2000). All 35 inputs are then standardised to mean zero and population SD one (ddof=0). An unstable direct power fit is retried after median/IQR rescaling; the fitted parameters, fallback details and skewness are recorded. No plausible extremes are clipped or removed from the primary dataset. Normality is not a requirement of PCA, and these transformations do not guarantee normality or eliminate influential observations. Median imputation can alter variances and covariances.

Table 6 reports actual imputation counts. Figure 3 shows the transformation diagnostic, while complete parameter and validation audits remain in the numerical exports. Missing metadata is preserved, and only selected inputs are imputed and scaled. The combined CSV retains 62 columns, while the separate numeric matrix has 35.

3.4 PCA extraction and component retention¶

PCA is fitted to the full retained environmental matrix for descriptive analysis (Jolliffe & Cadima, 2016). Column shuffling supplies 50 parallel-analysis permutations with seed 42, and each observed eigenvalue is compared with its ranked 95th-percentile null value (Horn, 1965). Parallel analysis is the explicit retention rule; the Kaiser eigenvalue-above-one count is a comparison (Kaiser, 1960). The earlier minimum-of-both expression remains selectable as legacy_min and its result is reported for transparency. Both rules retain seven components for these data.

Each axis is oriented so that its largest-magnitude eigenvector entry is positive. The fitted model itself is oriented so reloaded model scores agree. Loadings retain the earlier eigenvector × sqrt(sample eigenvalue) convention, approximating correlations within sqrt(n/(n−1)) because preprocessing uses population SD. Squared eigenvector weights give contributions summing to 100% per axis. Five components are interpreted in detail, with all retained axes shown where relevant.

3.5 Bleaching contrasts, source interpretation and validation¶

High-versus-Low contrasts use AUC, Cliff's δ = 2AUC−1, sample-size-weighted Cohen's d and group medians; Spearman correlation and three-group Kruskal–Wallis epsilon-squared are supporting descriptions. The older equal-weight-group-SD variable contrast is preserved under a separate label. Original Welch mean-difference intervals, BH-FDR adjustments (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), and sample-level Hotelling tests are retained as legacy nominal comparisons in the machine-readable statistical exports. They are not treated as valid independence-adjusted inference under repeated sites.

In particular, 196 sites occur in both High and Low groups. The former independent Welch test on site means does not resolve that overlap. The uncertainty audit instead resamples the union of sites using common site weights in both groups for 1,000 seeded resamples, reporting pointwise percentile 95% intervals for the same difference of site means. Resampling whole clusters preserves within-site dependence (Deen & de Rooij, 2020). Intervals condition on the fitted transforms/PCA, assume independence between sites and are not multiplicity-adjusted.

Categorical omega-squared is descriptive; categories with <50 events are pooled as Other. Within-source δ requires at least 30 High and 30 Low events per source and combines source statistics with High×Low pair weights. Comparisons of pooled and stratified estimates change the eligible population and weights; they do not isolate a causal percentage due to source. PCA is refitted for the four largest sources having at least 800 events. Congruence uses the original independent best absolute-cosine match, which need not be one-to-one.

Robustness checks retain twelve random site-half refits, a |Pearson r|≥0.90 pruning sensitivity, measured-depth-only contrasts, and a separate refit excluding |retained score|>10. Temporal descriptions use year correlations, sine/cosine month cycles by hemisphere, yearly median/IQRs for years with ≥30 events, and fixed within-period contrasts.

The compression diagnostic uses balanced logistic regression and five site-disjoint folds for two PCs, retained PCs and all inputs. Corrected CV fits medians, skew decisions, power parameters, scaling and PCA inside training folds using pre-imputation measurements. The globally fitted legacy comparison is preserved in the machine-readable statistical exports. Both evaluations condition on the fixed cohort, named study features and retained dimension; neither validates future-year performance, component selection itself, or an operational alert rule.

result = fit_pca(
    X,
    permutations=SETTINGS["parallel_permutations"],
    seed=SETTINGS["seed"],
    retention_rule=SETTINGS["retention_rule"],
)
if SETTINGS["n_interpret"] > result["n_retained"]:
    raise ValueError(
        "The interpreted component count exceeds the retained count."
    )
scores = result["scores"]
retained_scores = scores.iloc[:, : result["n_retained"]]
tables = analysis_tables(samples, X, result, SETTINGS["n_interpret"])
group_table = tables["pca_group_separation"]
comparison_columns = {
    name: retained_scores[name].to_numpy() for name in retained_scores
}
comparison_columns.update({name: X[name].to_numpy() for name in X})
tables["site_cluster_intervals"] = site_cluster_intervals(
    comparison_columns,
    samples.Bleaching_Group.to_numpy(),
    samples.Site_ID.to_numpy(),
    resamples=SETTINGS["bootstrap_resamples"],
    seed=SETTINGS["seed"],
)

3.6 Reproducibility and audit scope¶

This notebook runs from the raw file through preparation and PCA without executing another notebook first. The configuration cell supplies all settings, and functions live in the reusable modules. Readiness, fitted-transform reuse, reference comparisons and site-disjoint folds are checked during execution. Repeated raw-field listings, full legacy test tables, full fold logs and duplicate charts are omitted from the displayed report; their calculations and numerical exports remain available for inspection. Selected tables and figures appear with their discussion.

Run python scripts/execute_notebook.py consolidated_report_integrated.ipynb to execute the complete study and refresh its abstract. This version writes its own report, tables, figures and model to outputs/integrated_report/; it does not replace the original report copy.

4. Results and Discussion¶

4.1 Component retention and explained variance¶

Figure 4 and Table 7 distinguish variance compression from bleaching discrimination. Parallel analysis retains seven axes, compared with eight under the Kaiser rule; the first five provide the main interpretation. About nine components are needed for 80% variance and fourteen for 90%, so the environmental matrix contains several patterns rather than one dominant axis.

        result["n_parallel"],

})

4.2 Environmental interpretation¶

Figure 5 and Table 8 link each axis to measured variables and their temporal definitions. PC1 primarily describes longer-term stress history; PC2 contrasts typical thermal conditions and variability. PC3 emphasises survey-time anomalies and recent accumulated heat stress, while PC4 contrasts repeated recent stress with the site's longer-term thermal setting. PC5 is less clear-cut and mixes anomaly-frequency variability, maxima and distance to shore.

These labels are interpretations of loadings, not observed causal mechanisms. Thirty of the 35 inputs describe thermal conditions or stress, so thermal dominance partly reflects the representation of related variables. Original indicators remain useful alongside the components. The loading heatmap and component interpretation table provide the core evidence; repeated strongest-loading and family-share charts are omitted from this version.

4.3 Association with bleaching severity¶

The greatest environmental-variance axes are not the strongest bleaching contrasts. Table 9 shows weak pooled differences on PC1 and PC2, with larger contrasts on PC3 and PC4. Figure 6 shows substantial overlap between severity groups. The patterns describe tendencies across events rather than distinct clusters or deterministic classifications of individual reefs.

Table 10 gives the separate site-weighted uncertainty audit. Its positive PC3/PC4 intervals are consistent with a retained association under site resampling, but they do not establish causality or eliminate dependence between neighbouring sites. The sample-weighted effects and the site-weighted differences have different estimands and should not be numerically interchanged.

4.4 Source and geographic context¶

Source composition is strongly uneven. Table 11 shows that Donner contributes most High events, while several sources contain few or no High observations. Geographic categories and source labels are associated with component scores, especially the leading longer-term axes. Omega-squared and source stratification describe these relationships; they do not partition their overlapping causal contributions.

Figure 8 shows positive PC3 and PC4 contrasts inside each eligible source, with smaller combined stratified estimates than the pooled values. This supports source-aware interpretation of recent heat-stress associations, while the eligibility rule, weights and source-specific baselines limit direct pooled-versus-stratified comparisons. Source-loading congruence in Table 12 indicates recurring directions with substantial source variation; it does not prove absence of survey artifacts.

Table 11 also reports source-specific depth imputation. Figure 7 displays the categorical associations discussed here, including geography and source; these overlapping associations are descriptive.

4.5 Separation retained under compression and original indicators¶

The retained axes preserve about half the observed High-versus-Low squared Mahalanobis mean separation relative to all inputs (Table 13). This is a descriptive separation ratio, not a fraction of all bleaching information. The corrected, site-disjoint prediction diagnostic in Table 14 also finds better discrimination with all variables than with retained components, and the first two PCs alone perform worst. This is conditional evaluation of a fixed study design, not evidence for future-year or external-source performance.

Figure 9 presents the ten strongest original-variable contrasts, with recent heat-stress indicators among them. The original indicators should therefore be retained alongside component summaries. Their equal-weight-SD contrasts and the primary weighted Cohen's d have separate labels.

4.6 Robustness, depth and temporal interpretation¶

Table 15 summarises sampling, correlation-pruning and extreme-score sensitivities. No sensitivity exclusion alters the primary dataset. Depth missingness is source-related; Table 16 compares all-event contrasts with measured-depth-only contrasts. Stability of major directions is useful evidence of descriptive repeatability, not proof of unbiased source representation or an independent causal process.

Figure 10 describes annual component distributions. Site composition, seasonal coverage and unequal sample sizes change over time; score shifts alone are not a warming trend. Tables 17 and 18 supply year correlations, hemisphere-specific annual-cycle R², and within-period contrasts. The additional month-coloured scatterplots repeat the same score representation and are omitted. Date and geographic fields remain outside PCA throughout.

tables["robustness_congruence"], robustness_summary = robustness_checks(
    X,
    samples,
    result,
    SETTINGS["n_interpret"],
    SETTINGS["seed"],
    SETTINGS["extreme_score"],
)
tables["depth_sensitivity"] = depth_sensitivity(
    samples, scores.iloc[:, : SETTINGS["n_interpret"]]
)
tables["robustness_pruned_features"] = pd.DataFrame(
    {"feature": robustness_summary["pruned_columns"]}
)
tables["robustness_summary"] = pd.Series(
    {
        name: value
        for name, value in robustness_summary.items()
        if name != "pruned_columns"
    },
    name="value",
).to_frame()
tables["extreme_score_counts"] = (
    retained_scores.abs()
    .gt(SETTINGS["extreme_score"])
    .sum()
    .rename("extreme_events")
    .to_frame()
)
tables["depth_imputation_by_group"] = samples.groupby(
    "Bleaching_Group"
).Depth_m_was_missing.agg(["sum", "mean"])

4.7 Numerical Validation and Report Export¶

The report retains the same analytical cohort, preprocessing rules, feature list and PCA as the original version. A checksum-tied numerical comparison verifies primary results before export; changed inputs are reported as incomparable rather than silently passing a stale reference. The saved model reproduces the oriented scores, the raw source is preserved, and every CV fold keeps sites separate. Machine-readable audits support reproducibility without long on-screen listings.

The following checks and export complete the executable analysis. They create no additional on-screen audit tables and preserve this version's results separately from the original report.

tables["reference_validation"] = compare_reference(ROOT, result, tables)
tables["raw_data_profile"] = raw_profile
tables["raw_source_profile"] = raw_sources
tables["cohort_audit"] = retention
tables["preprocessing_readiness"] = readiness
report_dir = ROOT / "outputs" / "integrated_report"
exports = export_analysis(
    ROOT,
    samples,
    result,
    tables,
    figures,
    SETTINGS,
    pca_metadata,
    output_dir=report_dir,
)
(report_dir / "abstract.md").write_text(
    abstract_markdown(samples, result, tables) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
)
(report_dir / "conclusion.md").write_text(
    conclusion_markdown(samples, result, tables) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
)
assert file_sha256(ROOT / "coral.csv") == RAW_HASH
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    result["model"].transform(X.to_numpy()), scores, rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-10
)
print(
    f"Completed: {len(samples):,} events, {len(features)} PCA inputs and"
    f" {len(figures)} integrated figures; validation passed."
)
print(
    "This version's report and numerical exports are in"
    " outputs/integrated_report/."

Completed: 23,069 events, 35 PCA inputs and 10 integrated figures; validation passed.
This version's report and numerical exports are in outputs/integrated_report/.

5. Conclusion¶

The following conclusion is generated from the current fitted results and answers the primary question directly. It combines covariance compression with the separate bleaching-association evidence.

display(Markdown(conclusion_markdown(samples, result, tables)))

Answer to the research question: partly. For this cohort, PCA reveals an interpretable environmental structure associated with bleaching severity, but it provides an incomplete summary of the observed bleaching-group differences. Across 23,069 events, 7 retained components explain 75.9% of environmental variance. PC4 and PC3 show the strongest pooled High-versus-Low contrasts (PC4: δ = +0.47; PC3: δ = +0.44). These associations should be read with the source-stratified comparisons and uncertainty audits, because component scores also vary with source and geography. The retained components preserve 50.5% of the sample-level squared Mahalanobis separation between High and Low relative to all original inputs. This is a descriptive separation ratio, not a measure of predictive accuracy. The findings support retaining original environmental indicators alongside the component summaries. They do not establish causal effects, operational warning thresholds, or independent future-year performance.

6. Limitations, Recommendations and Future Work¶

The labelled-outcome and 1998-onward restrictions define the population represented by the results. Excluded events can differ systematically from retained events; the findings should not be generalised to unobserved reefs or earlier periods without checking that difference.

Source imbalance and heterogeneous field protocols affect both environments represented and bleaching encodings. Collecting more High-bleaching observations outside the dominant source, and evaluating source-held-out or independently collected observations, would strengthen assessment of transportability. A smaller stratified contrast does not identify a causal source contribution.

Repeated surveys at the same site violate simple observation-level independence. Site-cluster intervals improve the overlap audit but assume independence between sites, condition on fitted axes and provide no multiplicity-adjusted significance guarantee. Spatial dependence and fitting uncertainty remain for future work. The legacy nominal tests are documented for comparison.

Median imputation and source-related depth gaps can alter covariance and centralise observations. Sensitivity results should accompany interpretation, and fuller depth measurements would reduce reliance on imputation. Zero-heavy environmental inputs retain some skew after transformation; the power transformation neither establishes normality nor eliminates influence.

Thermal fields constitute most of the feature set, so their leading-component prominence partly reflects representation. Keep original indicators alongside PCA summaries and examine alternative scientifically justified feature balances before treating component prominence as ecological importance.

Some environmental variables summarise historical windows that differ from observation dates; day 15 is a documented substitute and some unit labels are inconsistent with stored values. The original units and records should be verified before raw-unit thresholds or time-sensitive applications. The conditional grouped CV does not resolve future availability of historical summary variables or validate a monitoring threshold.

The practical contribution is an interpretable, reproducible description of environmental variation and its observed bleaching associations. Recent heat-stress indicators are reasonable candidates for further monitoring validation. Operational alerts, causal protection benefits and forecasting claims require separate external and temporal evidence.
